newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine to sell 51 pct stake of jeep-maker plant.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine to sell 51 pct stake of jeep-maker plant.

text.p: Ukraine's state privatisation agency said on Tuesday it will sell a majority stake of the country's sole jeep-making plant in the western city of Lutsk.
State Property Fund (FDM) said in a statement it had opened a tender of investment programmes for the LuAZ plant on the Polish border 380 km (210 miles) west of Kiev.

"We badly need investments. Earlier we were talking about six million dollars but now we'd agree to four million dollars in investment," Vitaly Palyukh, head of LuAZ's privatisation department, told Reuters by telephone.
"The package of offered shares was recently unified. Earlier we planned to sell three stakes of 20 percent each but now we are offering a single stake of 51 percent," he added.
The FDM said the state would still keep the 25.1 percent stake.
The charter capital of LuAZ, which produces light four-wheel-drive jeep vehicles called the Volyn, is 18.9 million hryvnias ($10.2 million).
In the first quarter the plant produced 116 vehicles, which sell for about $5,000 each, compared to 15,000 in 1990 which is a year before the former Soviet Union fell apart.
"Now it's one of the worst enterprises in the car-making industry," the FDM statement said.
The former Soviet republic has three other vehicle makers.
South Korean Deawoo Group DWGR.CN and U.S. General Motors are forming a joint venture to produce cars at the AvtoZAZ plant in the eastern industrial city of Zaporizhya.
Italy's IVECO is involved in a joint venture with the KRAZ plant in the central Ukrainian city of Kremenchuk producing small trucks.
The LAZ bus-maker, located in the western city of Lviv, has been cooperating with French Renault for many years.
Palyukh said LuAZ's customers were mostly in the Russian Far East, Siberia, Central Asia, as well as central rural parts of Russia which have mainly dirt roads.
"Our main market was the Soviet Union and we have lost customers. Then we lost state support. Now we have do not have enough money and cannot develop production lines ourselves," Palyukh said.
The plant employed 3,000 workers in 1995 but currently employs about 2,300.
He added that the Russian car-maker GAZ and some Polish private investors had expressed interest.
"Proposals from western automobile giants haven't gone beyond the stage of telexes and faxes," Palyukh said.
